quotes.text: the sound of their work is really something to behold; a cocktail of basic 60's rock, basic 60's pop and Southern blues and "swamp" music, with a really great guitar sound, that ends up largely defying the ability to pigeonhole them into any one of those ingredient genres.

Basically, it's a sound that was seemingly made to make rock'n'roll 'purists' gush about the band and how they were "carriers of the rock'n'roll torch" during the late 60's and psychedelia and whatever.
John Fogerty was an amazing songwriter about 70% of the time (which is ten times as often as most bands), and he did have an awesome guitar sound for the kind of music he wrote for the band.

the instrumental breaks have such a subtle intensity that they manage to almost make me forget that they're taking a very basic (albeit great) blues-rocker and making it eight-and-a-half minutes long.

some of the backing vocals are sufficiently off-kilter that they almost border on "psychedelic," which seems kinda odd given that seemingly every fan or critic in the world likes to harp on how they were the "psychedelia-free" alternative for late 60's music.

Between 1968 and 1972, CCR knocked out seven albums and added a whole pile of songs to the rock canon: "Fortunate Son," "Bad Moon Rising," "Have You Ever Seen The Rain?," "Proud Mary," "Lookin' Out My Back Door," "Run Through The Jungle," "Born On The Bayou."
Creedence Clearwater Revival started as a teenage rock 'n' roll band in the Bay Area in the late '50s, and they released a few '60s garage rock singles as the Golliwogs.
Anyone who has ever watched a Vietnam movie knows that the Creedence catalog remains hugely lucrative, and it's cool that the man who wrote those songs now gets to say what will happen with them.
